newsitem.title: USA: Chances slim for Flinn upgrade, says Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Chances slim for Flinn upgrade, says Pentagon.

text.p: The Pentagon said on Tuesday that chances were "quite slim" that Air Force pilot Kelly Flinn could win an honourable discharge after resigning last week to avoid a court martial on adultery and other charges.

"The chances of receiving an honourable discharge in a situation like this are quite slim," said Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon, noting that fewer than 10 percent of such recent appeals had been granted by the Air Force.

Bacon also told reporters that neither Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall, who forced Flinn to accept a less-favourable general discharge, nor any future secretary would rule on any appeal by Flinn for an upgrade to an honourable discharge.

Flinn is expected to leave the service within days from her job flying B-52 bombers at Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota, where she reached an agreement with the Air Force last Thursday to avoid trial on criminal charges.

Flinn, 26 and single, had been charged with breaking the service's strict sexual code by having an affair with the husband of an enlisted woman, having a sexual fling with an enlisted man, lying about her conduct during an investigation and disobeying a direct order.

But in avoiding trial, the nation's first woman B-52 bomber pilot will have to repay the service up to $19,000 for part of her education and will get no veteran's benefits under the terms of her resignation.

Because Flinn accepted a general discharge and "resigned in lieu of a court martial" -- a step known as "RILO" in the Air Force -- she will also lose all medical and other special benefits that veterans receive, said the officials, who asked not to be identified.

"Basically, that is her right," Bacon told reporters when asked on Tuesday about indications from Flinn's lawyers that she might appeal for an honourable discharge after Widnall left the Pentagon and was replaced by a new secretary in the future.
But Bacon stressed that such appeals are handled by a review board of Air Force officers and that the secretary, the civilian leader of the service, takes no part in the process.
"There is a procedure. It goes to a discharge review board and the board generally takes anywhere from six to 18 months to rule on a request for an upgraded discharge," he said.

"The fact is that this is considered by a board that has been set up to review such petitions and it doesn't go to the secretary of the Air Force. In fact, if there is a review from the board proceeding, it goes to a federal court, not to the secretary," Bacon added.

Widnall told reporters last week that she refused to accept Flinn's offer to leave with an honourable discharge but granted her a general discharge, which does not carry the stigma and conditions of a dishonourable discharge.
